prompt: `x` is an `int`. What is the type of `p` after `p := &x`?
hint: `%T` printed it in section 02.

choices.text: `&int`
choices.why: `&` makes an address in an expression; in a type, "pointer to" is written with `*`.

choices.text: `*int`
choices.why: Right. `*int` is "pointer to an `int`", and `%T` printed exactly that.

choices.text: `int`, a second variable holding 21
choices.why: That is what `p := x` would make. `&x` is the address, not a copy of the number.

choices.text: `pointer`, a type of its own shared by every address
choices.why: A Go pointer carries the type it points at; `*int` and `*string` are different types.

prompt: After `x := 21` and `p := &x`, the statement `___ = 30` sets `x` to 30 without naming `x`.
hint: Follow the pointer, on the left of `=`.

prompt: `var p *int` followed by `fmt.Println(*p)`. What happens?
hint: What is a pointer's zero value, and what is at that address?

choices.text: It prints 0, the zero value of an `int`
choices.why: There is no `int` to read: `p` is nil and points at no variable at all.

choices.text: It prints `<nil>`
choices.why: That is what printing `p` itself gives. `*p` tries to follow it.

choices.text: It panics: invalid memory address or nil pointer dereference
choices.why: Right. Following a nil pointer stops the program, at run time, with exit status 2.

choices.text: The compiler refuses `*p`, because it sees a pointer that was never given a value
choices.why: It compiled; whether `p` is nil is only known while the program runs.

prompt: `p := &nums[0]` points into an array of three `int`. Why does the compiler refuse `p++`?
hint: Read the error: `non-numeric type *int`.

choices.text: Because `p++` might step past the end of the array
choices.why: The refusal has nothing to do with where `p` points; `p++` is refused on any pointer.

choices.text: Because a pointer is not a number, and Go has no pointer arithmetic
choices.why: Right. To reach the next element you index the array, `nums[1]`.

choices.text: Because `++` is reserved for variables declared with `var`
choices.why: `*a++` worked in section 02 on a pointer from a function; `++` cares about the type, not the declaration.

choices.text: Because arrays are values, so their elements have no addresses
choices.why: `&nums[0]` compiled on the line before; array elements do have addresses.

prompt: `func newPlayer(name string) *Player { p := Player{Name: name}; return &p }`. A reviewer used to C says the returned pointer dangles once the function returns. What is true?
hint: What did `newCounter` print in section 02?

choices.text: It dangles; the function has to use `new(Player)` instead
choices.why: `new(Player)` and `&p` give the same guarantee: the variable lives while it is reachable.

choices.text: It is safe for structs, and it would dangle for an `int`
choices.why: `newCounter` returned the address of a local `int`, and both counters kept working.

choices.text: It is safe: `p` lives for as long as the returned pointer reaches it
choices.why: Right. A Go variable lives while something can reach it; lesson 24 shows where the compiler puts it.

choices.text: The compiler refuses to return the address of a local variable
choices.why: `newCounter` did exactly that and compiled.

prompt: `p` is a `*Player`. What does `p.Score++` do?
hint: Go has no `->`.

choices.text: It changes a copy of the player, as lesson 22's `win` did
choices.why: Lesson 22's `win` received a `Player`. Through a pointer the change reaches the player it points at.

choices.text: Nothing: it is refused, and the field needs `(*p).Score++`
choices.why: The long form compiles too, and nobody writes it, because the dot follows the pointer.

choices.text: It moves `p` to the next field of the struct
choices.why: There is no pointer arithmetic; `++` applies to the field.

choices.text: It increments the `Score` of the player `p` points at
choices.why: Right. `p.Score` on a pointer means `(*p).Score`.

prompt: `bia := &Player{Name: "Bia", Score: 1}` and `twin := &Player{Name: "Bia", Score: 1}`. What do `bia == twin` and `*bia == *twin` print?
hint: One compares addresses, the other compares structs.

choices.text: `true true`, since the two players are equal
choices.why: The players are equal, and they are two variables, so their addresses differ.

choices.text: `false true`
choices.why: Right. Two `&Player{...}` make two variables; following both compares the fields.

choices.text: `false false`, because pointers to structs are never equal
choices.why: `p == &x` was `true` in section 02: pointers are equal when they lead to one variable.

choices.text: A compile error: structs cannot be compared
choices.why: A struct whose fields are comparable compares with `==`, field by field.

prompt: `ana` is a variable of type `Player`. Which of these expressions have the type `*Player`? Choose all that apply.
hint: Section 03 named three ways to get one.

choices.text: `&ana`
choices.why: Yes: the address of a variable that already exists.

choices.text: `&Player{Name: "Bia"}`
choices.why: Yes: a struct made on the spot, and its address.

choices.text: `new(Player)`
choices.why: Yes: a zero `Player` and its address.

choices.text: `Player{}`
choices.why: No: that is a `Player` value, with no address taken.

choices.text: `*ana`
choices.why: No: `*` follows a pointer, and `ana` is not one, so this does not compile.

prompt: `Options{Limit: &10}` is refused with `cannot take address of 10`. Why?
hint: What does `&` need on its right?

choices.text: `Limit` is a `*int`, and 10 is an untyped constant that has no type yet
choices.why: The message is about the address, not the type; `new(10)` turns the same constant into an `int` happily.

choices.text: `&` needs a variable, and a constant is not one
choices.why: Right. Before Go 1.26 the fix was `n := 10` and `&n`; now `new(10)` makes the variable.

choices.text: `&` is not allowed inside a struct literal
choices.why: `Limit: &n` inside the literal is the older, working form.

choices.text: Pointer fields are only set after the struct is made
choices.why: A literal sets them like any other field: `Options{Limit: new(10)}` ran.

prompt: `new(10)` compiles in a module whose `go` line says 1.___ or later.
hint: The compiler said so when the line was set to 1.25.

prompt: Why does the compiler refuse `&ages["ana"]` on a `map[string]int`?
hint: What does `grow` do to the old table?

choices.text: Because map values are constants once stored
choices.why: `ages["ana"] = 31` changes one; the refusal is about the address.

choices.text: Because a map moves its entries to a new table when it grows
choices.why: Right. A pointer to an element would lead into a table the map had discarded.

choices.text: Because a map is a pointer already, so `&` would be redundant
choices.why: The map value is a pointer to the table; an element inside the table is something else.

choices.text: Because only struct elements of a map have addresses
choices.why: `players["ana"].Score = 11` was refused too: no element of a map is a variable.

prompt: `players` is a `map[string]Player`, and `players["ana"].Score = 11` is refused. Which of these compiles and changes Ana's score?
hint: Treat the stored struct as a value: read it, change it, put it back.

choices.text: `(&players["ana"]).Score = 11`
choices.why: A map element has no address, so `&players["ana"]` is refused too.

choices.text: `players["ana"]->Score = 11`
choices.why: Go has no `->`; that is C's spelling.

choices.text: `p := players["ana"]; p.Score = 11; players["ana"] = p`
choices.why: Right. The copy is a variable, so its field is assignable, and storing it back replaces the entry.

choices.text: `*players["ana"].Score = 11`
choices.why: `Score` is an `int`, not a pointer, so there is nothing for `*` to follow.

prompt: `nums := make([]int, 3, 10)`, `first := &nums[0]`, `nums = append(nums, 4)`, `*first = 100`. What is `nums[0]`?
hint: Compare the capacity here with section 04's.

choices.text: 100, because `append` had room and did not move the slice
choices.why: Right. With capacity 10, the 4 went into the same array, and `first` still points into it.

choices.text: 0, because `append` always moves a slice to a new array
choices.why: It moves only when the capacity is used up; lesson 12 showed both cases.

choices.text: A panic, because `first` points at a stale element
choices.why: Even a stale pointer does not panic; and here it is not stale at all.

choices.text: 0, since `first` was taken before the append and still points at the old array
choices.why: When it was taken matters only if the append moved the slice, and with room to spare it did not.

prompt: Put what happens in `~/pointers-stale` in order, from the pointer being taken to the write that `nums` never sees.
hint: The slice starts full: length 3, capacity 3.
items: `append` finds no room past the length
`append` copies the three elements to a new array and adds 4
`nums` is assigned the slice over the new array

prompt: `addTo(s *[]int, v int)` appends through a pointer. Which shape does the standard library use for functions that grow a slice?
hint: Look at `append` itself, and at `slices.Insert`.

choices.text: Taking `*[]T`, so callers do not have to assign anything
choices.why: That is `addTo`'s shape; `append` and `slices.Insert` take a slice and return one.

choices.text: Returning the new slice, which the caller stores
choices.why: Right. `s = append(s, v)` shows at the call that `s` changes.

choices.text: Returning a pointer to the new array
choices.why: A slice already carries that pointer, with its length and capacity.

choices.text: Neither: slices are passed by reference, so the caller sees the growth
choices.why: Lesson 22 took that picture apart; the caller's length is in the caller's own slice value.

prompt: Match each piece of syntax with what it means.
hint: The star means one thing in a type and another in an expression.

pairs.right: the address of the variable x
the variable that p points at
a pointer that leads to no variable

right_distractors: the int stored right after x in memory

prompt: `func reset(p *Player) { p = &Player{} }` is called as `reset(&ana)`, with Ana's score at 10. What is `ana.Score` afterwards?
hint: Did the function write through `p`, or to `p`?

choices.text: 0, because the function received Ana's address and replaced what was there
choices.why: It received the address and then replaced its copy of it, without writing through it.

choices.text: 10, because the function only changed its own copy of the pointer
choices.why: Right. It is lesson 22's `replace` again: assigning to a parameter never reaches the caller; `*p = Player{}` would.

choices.text: A panic, because the new player is freed on return
choices.why: Nothing panics; the new player is simply unreachable once `reset` returns.

choices.text: A compile error: a pointer parameter is read-only
choices.why: A parameter is an ordinary variable, pointer or not, and assigning to it compiles.

prompt: `byName := map[string]*Player{"ana": &ana}`, then `byName["ana"].Score = 50`. What is `ana.Score`?
hint: What did the map store: a player, or an address?

choices.text: Unchanged, because a map stores a copy of what you put in it
choices.why: It stored a copy of the pointer, and the copy leads to `ana` itself.

choices.text: Nothing: assigning to a field through a map is refused
choices.why: That refusal is for `map[string]Player`. Here the element is a pointer, and the field belongs to a variable.
Right. The map holds `&ana`, so the dot follows it to `ana` and writes there.

choices.text: Unchanged until the map is stored back with `byName["ana"] = p`
choices.why: Storing back is the fix for a map of structs; with pointers the write has already landed.

prompt: In a module whose `go` line is 1.27.1, which of these compile? `nums` is a `[]int`, `ages` a `map[string]int`, `ana` a `Player` and `p := &ana`. Choose all that apply.
hint: Addresses of slice elements, yes; of map elements, no; arithmetic, never.

choices.why: Yes: a slice element is a variable with an address.

choices.text: `a := &ages["ana"]`
choices.why: No: a map element has no address, because the map moves it.

choices.text: `p.Score = 3`
choices.why: Yes: the dot follows `p` to `ana`.
No: Go has no pointer arithmetic.
Yes: `new` takes an expression from Go 1.26 on.

prompt: When should a function take a `*Player` instead of a `Player`?
hint: Section 03 gave two reasons, both from lesson 22.

choices.text: Every time, because copying a struct is slow
choices.why: Lesson 22 measured a small struct copying inside the cost of the call.

choices.text: Whenever it reads more than one field of the player it was given
choices.why: Reading fields works the same on a copy; the number of fields read is not the question.

choices.text: When it must change the caller's player, or the struct is large
choices.why: Right. Otherwise the copy keeps the caller's player out of the function's reach.

choices.text: Never: pointers to structs are unsafe in Go
choices.why: Go pointers have no arithmetic and keep their target alive; `win(&ana)` is ordinary Go.
